## The scene

![The planar step scene, +x to the left as in the paper. The box has four edges and four vertices; the disk has its boundary. The environment is one object E: its edges E:L (floor), E:S (riser) and E:P (platform), and its one convex vertex, the step corner v<sub>S</sub> = E:S/P.](media/step1_scene.svg){.lightbox}

Three bodies move or touch in the x–z plane:

- **the manipulator M**, a disk of radius r = a/8, driven by two slide motors
  of ±1 N each;
- **the object B**, a square box of side a = 125 mm and weight 0.98 N;
- **the environment E**, one polygon: floor, riser of height h = a/4, and
  platform.

The features of a body are its edges and its convex vertices; the disk has
one feature, its circle. E's convex vertices are found from the geometry,
so only the step corner qualifies. The concave floor–riser junction is not
a feature: Xiao and Ji count a convex element pressed into a concave corner
as one contact with each of the two edges.

A **template** is a pair of features on two different bodies that may
touch. The catalog has 40: 8 disk–box (the disk against the box's 4 edges
and 4 vertices) and 32 box–environment (the box's 8 features against E's 4).
Seven have names, used throughout:

| Name | Template | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| g | (−z<sub>B</sub>, E:L) | box bottom flat on the floor |
| g<sub>v</sub> | (v<sub>+−</sub>, E:L) | box corner on the floor |
| s | (+x<sub>B</sub>, E:S) | box side flush on the riser |
| s<sub>v</sub> | (+x<sub>B</sub>, v<sub>S</sub>) | box side on the step corner |
| t | (+x<sub>B</sub>, E:P) | box side on the platform (the landed box) |
| m<sub>x</sub>, m<sub>z</sub> | (∂M, −x<sub>B</sub>), (∂M, −z<sub>B</sub>) | disk on a box face |

The paper also counts four disk–environment templates (44 in all); the
code leaves them out.

## Principal contacts

Closed features share their boundaries. When the box sits flat on the
floor, its bottom edge touches the floor, and so do its two bottom vertices
and the lower ends of its sides. Counting every touching pair would light
several templates for one physical contact.

Xiao and Ji's **principal contact** fixes this (Xiao 1993; Xiao and Ji,
*IJRR* 2001, Def. 1): a contact between two features counts only if it is
not the boundary of a contact between higher-dimensional features. Flat on
the floor, the box realizes {g}; tilted onto its corner, {g<sub>v</sub>}. A
**formation** is a set of templates; a pose *realizes* a formation when the
formation is exactly its set of principal contacts. Formations are what the
planner searches over.

Between two convex elements there is at most one principal contact at a
time. The box can touch the floor and the riser at once ({g, s} in the
corner), but not the floor with two edges.

## The recognizer

Simulated poses never touch exactly: contacts sink a little into each other
and float a little apart. The recognizer labels a pose with tolerances
ε<sub>on</sub> = 1 mm (separation) and ε<sub>pen</sub> (overlap). The
**contact set** K<sub>c</sub> of a template lies on the box's feature and
depends on the other feature:

- against an edge of E: the part within ε<sub>on</sub> of the edge, or
  sunk into E across it (an interval);
- against a vertex of E: the point of the box's feature closest to it;
- against the disk: the point of the box's feature closest to the disk's
  center.

A template is **on** when:

1. **In band.** Its gap lies between −ε<sub>pen</sub> and ε<sub>on</sub>, and
   K<sub>c</sub> is not empty.
2. **It touches interiors.** The touching part is not only at an edge's end
   that is itself a vertex feature of the same body. For example, a box
   resting on v<sub>S</sub> alone is s<sub>v</sub>, not t or s.
3. **Edge on edge needs alignment.** The two edges are parallel within
   θ<sub>e</sub> and overlap by at least ℓ<sub>min</sub> = a/16 = 7.8 mm.
4. **The larger contact wins.** K<sub>c</sub> is not contained, within
   ε<sub>on</sub>, in the contact set of a higher-dimensional template of
   the same pair that is also on.

The tilt tolerance is derived, not tuned: θ<sub>e</sub> = arcsin(ε<sub>on</sub>/L<sub>e</sub>)
≈ 1.83°, where L<sub>e</sub> = h is the shortest edge in an edge–edge
template. On the riser that is the angle at which the far end of the
overlap leaves the 1 mm band, so the test agrees with the point-contact
test of physics engines there. Using one angle rather than a contact length
makes a box flush in the step corner lose its floor and riser contacts at
the same tilt; a contact-length rule switched them at different tilts and
labeled the impossible {g<sub>v</sub>, s} in between.

**Ambiguous poses.** If the tolerances leave two contacts that cannot
coexist (the same pair of convex elements, or one containing the other),
the recognizer reports the higher-dimensional one, then the smaller gap,
then catalog order, and counts the tie. A tied pose is never a search node
or a solver success. Ties happen under deep overlap: ε<sub>pen</sub> = 5 mm
is provisional, and 257 of 4,000 jittered demo poses tie at that value
(475 at 10 mm) ([Issues](issues.qmd#eps-pen)).

**Correctness.** The paper proves that within η<sub>max</sub> ≈ 0.35 mm of
an exact pose that is well away from degenerate configurations, the
recognizer returns exactly the exact principal contacts and the pose is not
ambiguous. An independent check ran the code on 207,208 such poses and
found no counterexample.

## Validity

A formation is **valid** if some admissible pose realizes it. Validity is
computed from the geometry (Decision 11): each formation's contact equations
are solved or certified infeasible, and every valid one has a witness pose
whose label is recomputed there. On the step, **357** formations are valid;
58,688 are invalid with a certificate and 4 are decided numerically. Validity
is hereditary (every subset of a valid formation is valid), so it is
reproduced exactly by its minimal excluded sets, which make the test a few
matrix products over any batch of formations.

Two more rules make a valid formation a search node: a vertex-on-vertex
contact appears only as its object pair's sole contact, and the formation must
be **recognizable** (some exact realization is read by the tolerant recognizer
as exactly that formation, without a tie). That leaves **328** formations,
reproduced by 561 minimal excluded sets (560 pairs and 1 triple); none of the
removed ones is on the step chain or in the demo.

The four exclusions that an earlier hand-written table declared, {g, t},
{g<sub>v</sub>, s}, {g, s<sub>v</sub>} and {g, m<sub>z</sub>}, are now
derived (for example, {g, t} needs a tilt of 0° and 90° at once). That table
accepted 37,203 formations, among them impossible ones such as the box's bottom
on the floor and on the platform at once.

## Connected regions

Xiao and Ji define a contact state as a formation together with one
connected region of the poses that realize it. The search keys a node by
its formation, the disk's connected region given the box's pose, and the
box's pose within a merge radius ([Node identity](node-identity.qmd)), so it
matters whether a formation's region splits. Checked by sampling (scripts in `c-gnn`,
`reports/contact-mode-graphs/scripts/connectivity/`, at commit `9261ece`):

- each of the chain's eight formations is one component at link radii of
  20 and 40 mm, and at 5 and 10 mm too, except on a random half of the
  full-band samples, where {m<sub>x</sub>, s<sub>v</sub>} splits at 5 mm and
  {m<sub>z</sub>, t} at 10 mm;
- discovery found 285 formations and 89 were analysed; 18 showed several
  components at 20 or 40 mm, and 14 of those were densified. The two chain
  formations and 8 others are then one component at 20 and 40 mm; the empty
  formation splits on a random half at 20 mm; three with the box in the air
  hold together only at 40 mm; the 4 not densified still split at 20 or
  40 mm;
- 196 rarely sampled formations were not analysed, 87 of them containing a
  chain template.

This is sampling evidence that the chain's formations are connected at
link radii of 20 mm and more, not a proof.

## The demo, frame by frame

The viewer replays the 1,721-frame demo shipped with `cmg`
(`step_example_trajectory.npz`), labels every frame with the recognizer,
and draws the contact sets.

<iframe src="contact-viewer.html" title="Contact layer viewer" loading="lazy" allow="fullscreen" allowfullscreen
  style="width:100%;height:1260px;border:1px solid var(--bs-border-color, #d0d7de);border-radius:8px"></iframe>

[Open the viewer on its own page](contact-viewer.html){target="_blank"} for more room.

What to watch for:

- **One contact per pair of convex elements.** The "in band" column is the
  naive count of touching templates, up to 5 for one contact; the on column
  never holds more than one.
- **The chain, in order:** {g} → {m<sub>x</sub>, g} → {m<sub>x</sub>, g, s}
  → {m<sub>x</sub>, g<sub>v</sub>, s<sub>v</sub>} → {m<sub>x</sub>, s<sub>v</sub>}
  → {s<sub>v</sub>} → {t} → {m<sub>z</sub>, t} → {t}, in 15 runs of frames,
  with no invalid formation.
- **Two rocks.** At frame 609 the box hits the riser and rocks onto its
  corner (up to 2.6°); after landing (frames 708–712) it seesaws on the step
  corner, so only s<sub>v</sub> is on. Both are real motion.
- **Ties** fire on 2 frames, both with the box pressed more than 1 mm into
  the riser.

![Box tilt through the push into the riser, the pivot and the landing (frames 604–719); shading marks runs of one formation. While the disk pushes the box along the floor the tilt reaches 0.58° (the box sinks unevenly into the soft floor). The rock at the riser (2.6°) and the seesaw after landing (2.9°) cross θ<sub>e</sub> ≈ 1.83°. Near θ<sub>e</sub> a label can flicker for a few frames (623–625); hysteresis for trajectory labels waits for a noise model.](media/step1_tilt.svg){.lightbox}

## Reproduce

```bash
cd ~/repos/research/c-gnn && git switch phase1/planar && git pull && cd cmg
source .venv314/bin/activate      # Python 3.14; uv pip install -e ".[dev,cuda]" matplotlib
JAX_PLATFORMS=cpu PYTHONPATH=tests python -m pytest -q tests/test_planar_contact.py
JAX_PLATFORMS=cpu python <website>/research/nonprehensile/planar-build/scripts/01_contact_layer.py <out dir>
JAX_PLATFORMS=cpu python <website>/research/nonprehensile/planar-build/scripts/03_ties_eps_pen.py --out <out dir>/ties.json   # ties per ε_pen
```

The planar gap takes 22 ms per 7,680 poses on the CPU. CPU runs repeat
exactly; GPU runs repeat between processes only with
`XLA_FLAGS=--xla_gpu_deterministic_ops=true`.
